title: Relative clauses
tagline: One extra clause, two jobs: pin down exactly who or what you mean, or simply add more about it.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Writing Part 2 — stories and descriptive pieces
why: A relative clause can change what a sentence actually means: 'the students who arrived late missed the bus' is not the same claim as 'the students, who arrived late, missed the bus'. B2 First tests both the comma and the pronoun, and reduced relative clauses (-ing/-ed) are a quick way to sound less repetitive in Writing Part 2.

rows.label: Function
cells: identifies which person or thing we mean
adds extra information; the sentence still makes sense without it

rows.label: Can you omit the pronoun?
cells: yes, if it is the object of the clause

rows.label: Example
cells: The teacher who marked our essays is strict.
Miss Vega, who marked our essays, is strict.

diagrams.title: Reducing a relative clause

before.text: The scientist who was leading the project resigned in March.

after.text: The scientist leading the project resigned in March.

steps: Remove the relative pronoun and the auxiliary 'be'.
Keep the -ing form to show an active, ongoing action.
Use the -ed form instead if the meaning is passive.

head: Use
Pattern
Example
rows: The student who forgot his badge waited outside.
The essay (that) she wrote won first prize.
Cusco, which is in the Andes, gets cold at night.
The girl whose bag was stolen reported it at once.
the school where we study English
the reason why she left the team
which + comment on the clause before it
He passed the exam, which surprised everyone.

use.point: Defining relative clauses: saying exactly which one

examples.text: The boy who scored the winning goal is in our class.
Is this the app that Liam recommended for learning vocabulary?
examples.note: that can replace which for things

examples.text: Students whose parents work abroad often video-call every day.
Nadia, who moved here from Trujillo, still supports her old team.
examples.note: commas — could be removed without losing the main fact

examples.text: The Andes, which stretch along the whole country, shape Peru's climate.
The match was cancelled, which annoyed everyone on the team.
examples.note: which refers to the whole previous idea, not a single noun

examples.text: The club which Sofia belongs to meets on Thursdays.
The club to which Sofia belongs meets on Thursdays.
The teacher who I spoke to gave me some useful advice.
The girl sitting next to Mateo is his cousin.
The photos taken during the trip are on the school website.

watch_out.wrong: Miss Vega who teaches us English is from Arequipa.
watch_out.right: Miss Vega, who teaches us English, is from Arequipa.
watch_out.why: A name is already specific, so the clause is non-defining and needs commas.

watch_out.wrong: The book, that I borrowed, was really long.
watch_out.right: The book that I borrowed was really long.
watch_out.why: You can't use that in a non-defining clause, and this clause is actually defining, so it takes no commas.

watch_out.wrong: The man who he lives next door plays the guitar.
watch_out.right: The man who lives next door plays the guitar.
watch_out.why: Don't repeat the subject with he — the relative pronoun already does that job.

watch_out.wrong: This is the app who Liam recommended.
watch_out.right: This is the app that / which Liam recommended.
watch_out.why: Who is only for people; use that or which for things.

watch_out.wrong: The house who's roof is blue belongs to my uncle.
watch_out.right: The house whose roof is blue belongs to my uncle.
watch_out.why: Whose (possession) is often confused with who's (who is / who has).

watch_out.wrong: I met a student, that comes from Canada.
watch_out.right: I met a student who comes from Canada.
watch_out.why: This information identifies which student, so no comma and no that needed here — but if you keep the comma, use who, not that.

dialogue.title: Planning the Cusco trip
dialogue.context: Mateo, Sofia and Nadia are choosing which sites to visit on the school history trip, with Miss Vega checking the final list.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I found a guide who used to work at the site — he's the one whose tours everyone recommends.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Perfect. Sacsayhuamán, which we studied last term, has to be on the list.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Agreed. And the market where we can buy souvenirs is right next to it.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: There's also that small museum that Liam mentioned — the one with the textiles.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Miss Vega, is this the museum which you visited last year?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It is. The curator, who studied in Lima, gives a short talk in English.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: The students whose Spanish is still basic will appreciate that.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: One thing though: the hostel we're staying at doesn't have wifi in every room.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That's fine — it's the view that matters, not the wifi.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: The reason why I chose this hostel is exactly that: fewer screens, more talking.

items.sentence: The coach ___ trains the under-16 team used to play professionally.
My cousin, ___ lives in Trujillo, is coming to visit next month.
items.why: that is not allowed after a comma

items.sentence: This is the laptop ___ screen cracked last week.
items.why: whose shows possession, even for things

items.sentence: The stadium ___ we watched the final is being rebuilt.
Nadia's essay, ___ won first prize, took her three weeks to write.
items.why: non-defining clause about a thing needs which, not that

items.sentence: I don't remember the exact day ___ we first met.
The teacher ___ I told you about is retiring this year.
items.why: object pronoun can be omitted in a defining clause

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with who, which, whose, where, when, why or that. If the pronoun can be omitted, write '–'.

items.sentence: The girl ___ sits next to me in Maths is Nadia's cousin.
Arequipa, ___ is known as the White City, sits below three volcanoes.
That's the shop ___ owner used to play for the national team.
The film ___ we watched in class last Friday was based on a true story.
This is the classroom ___ we do our Cambridge practice tests.
Can you tell me the reason ___ the match was postponed?
The summer ___ we travelled to the coast was unusually rainy.
Liam, ___ never misses training, was surprisingly late today.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Sofia wrote an essay. It won a national prize.
That's the boy. His father coaches the football team.
This is the café. We meet our friends there every Saturday.
I can't remember the exact date. We booked the trip on that date.
The girl was sitting by the window. She is Mateo's sister.
The documents were left on the desk. They belong to Miss Vega.

summary: A defining relative clause tells you which person or thing; a non-defining one adds extra information and needs commas.
Never use that after a comma — non-defining clauses need who, which, whose, where or when.
You can drop the pronoun only when it is the object of a defining clause: the book (that) I borrowed.
Which can also comment on a whole previous clause, not just one noun.
A reduced relative clause drops the pronoun and 'be': -ing for active meaning, -ed for passive.
